note: Survey of jailbreaking, data poisoning and personal-information leakage against language models, with the defences proposed so far. The natural companion to our AI Security section.
title: Security and Privacy Challenges of Large Language Models: A Survey

reading.body:
This survey catalogs jailbreaking, data poisoning, and personal-information leakage as the three main attack categories against language models, along with the defenses proposed for each.

Grouping these three together is itself informative, they target different points in a model's lifecycle, poisoning at training time, jailbreaking and leakage at inference time, which means no single defense covers all three. A system hardened against jailbreak prompts is not thereby protected against a poisoned training set, and a model that resists leaking training data may still be jailbroken through adversarial prompting.

As a survey, it aggregates other researchers' findings rather than reporting new attacks itself, and it does not say which of these three risks is most common in production deployments today.

explain_beginner: Chatbots and other AI language tools are built to be helpful and to keep certain information private, but this survey lays out three specific ways those protections can fail. The first is jailbreaking, tricking a model into ignoring its safety instructions, for example by asking it to roleplay a character with no restrictions. The second is data poisoning, secretly corrupting the material a model learns from so it behaves badly later without anyone noticing during normal use. The third is leaking private information, where an attacker can get a model to reveal snippets of the exact personal data it was trained on or exposed to. The authors reviewed dozens of published attack techniques and the defenses researchers have proposed for each, and looked at how these risks show up in real settings like hospitals, schools, and transportation systems. The paper does not resolve these problems, it maps out how serious and varied they already are, and where good defenses still do not exist.
explain_business: Any organization deploying a customer facing or internal LLM should read this survey as a checklist of specific, already demonstrated risks rather than a hypothetical concern. Jailbreak techniques exist that can be executed with fewer than twenty carefully crafted prompts, poisoning attacks can corrupt a model's behavior through fine tuning data without visible signs during testing, and memorization based extraction can pull private data straight out of a deployed model, all compliance relevant wherever GDPR, HIPAA, or similar regulations apply to the data involved. Because the authors find no standardized way to measure how well a given defense actually works, businesses cannot simply pick a mitigation off a vendor's feature list and assume it is adequate. They need independent red teaming appropriate to their own deployment before launch, and ongoing monitoring afterward, particularly in the healthcare and education contexts the survey specifically flags as high exposure areas.
explain_practitioner: This survey organizes published attacks on large language models into three categories, jailbreaking, data poisoning, and personally identifiable information extraction, and catalogs specific named methods for each, including DAN and GCG style suffix attacks for jailbreaking, TrojanPuzzle and AutoPoison for poisoning training or fine tuning data, and prefix based memorization attacks and multi step extraction prompts for pulling out PII such as emails or phone numbers. For each category it reviews corresponding defenses, input paraphrasing and perplexity filtering against jailbreaks, fine pruning and trigger detection methods like STRIP against poisoning, and differential privacy training such as DP-SGD against data leakage, then maps these risks onto deployment domains including healthcare, education, and transportation where HIPAA and GDPR style compliance concerns apply directly. The authors explicitly flag the absence of standardized metrics for comparing attack severity across studies as a major gap, meaning claims that one defense outperforms another are hard to verify consistently across the literature reviewed.
